verdicts.why: In the 'necessity is the mother of invention' sense the word names a figurative source or origin and takes no side on it; the book sentences show the kinship sense, but the gloss is binding and this sense describes without judging.
A written message is a plain thing named plainly; nothing about choosing 'letter' over 'note' or 'message' reveals the speaker's attitude.
An alphabetic character is a purely descriptive referent with no plainer neighbour to be preferred over and no attitude to carry.

'The letter' names the literal reading itself, and 'to the letter' is neutral or approving; the disapproval sometimes felt in 'the letter but not the spirit' comes from the explicit contrast, not from the word.

Chosen over the plain 'woman', 'lady' signals courtesy, deference and an assumption of gentility (the gloss itself says 'polite'), and in modern use can land as dated or patronising, so a learner needs to know how it lands.
As a title of rank for a peeress the word states a social fact rather than an attitude; 'Lady Catherine' describes her station without the speaker approving or disapproving of it.
